themes.label: Gun rights / gun reform policy advocacy
defining_features: primary_policy_domain: Guns/firearms; Second Amendment framing
policy_prescription_present: advocates specific gun reform or changes (permits, outlawing assault weapons, etc.)
call_to_action: urging action toward gun reform/rights
themes.interpretation: Many posts revolve around firearms regulation as a central moderation topic; some are policy-prescriptive and may also include sharper rhetoric, but the core theme is consistent policy debate/advocacy around guns and the Second Amendment.

themes.label: Strong anti-outgroup labeling and us-vs-them targeting
defining_features: us_vs_them_framing: explicit in-group vs out-group contrasts
ingroup_outgroup_labeling: pejorative partisan faction labels (e.g., Leftoids/Righties)
mirror_shift_direction or target_directionality: blame reassigned to opposing groups/actors
us_vs_them_insulting_group_labels: derogatory labels for supporters
themes.interpretation: A recurring moderation-relevant pattern is partisan or group-based devaluation: posts frame opponents as an outgroup, assign negative intent, and sometimes combine this with insults or categorical blame.

themes.label: Profanity / taboo slurs and intense personal or group insults
defining_features: profanity_or_taboo_language: explicit profanity (e.g., fuck, cunt) and derogatory taboo terms
dehumanizing_or_hate_style_insult: extreme dehumanizing labels (e.g., “human garbage”)
all_caps_emphasis: uppercase used alongside insults/accusations (often intensifying offensiveness)
high_punctuation_intensity: escalation with aggressive formatting
themes.interpretation: Profanity and dehumanizing insults are prominent in removed content, suggesting this feature cluster is a strong moderation signal even when political disagreement is otherwise present.

themes.label: Conspiracy / covert control / foreign agent narratives
defining_features: conspiratorial_framing: claims hidden influence or covert control (Russia, Putin, foreign puppeteers)
accusation_of_traitor_or_foreign_agent: labeling targets as foreign assets/traitors
factual_assertion_vs_speculation: denial of mainstream evidence via certainty or counterclaims (often used in conspiratorial contexts)
themes.interpretation: Posts that attribute political outcomes to hidden or foreign manipulation appear frequently in the removed group, indicating conspiracy framing is often treated as higher-risk (especially when paired with hostile rhetoric).

themes.label: Normative moral language about rights, fairness, and harm
defining_features: normative_moral_language: moral judgments (rights not debatable, insanity, justice/autonomy, murder claims)
victimhood_or_persecution_framing: portray groups as victims/under attack and blame opponents
causal_claim_present: moralized causality (under attack, harms attributed to actors)
themes.interpretation: Many kept posts lean heavily on moral reasoning and victim/persecution framing. While not always moderated, this cluster signals emotionally charged normative claims that often co-occur with other risk features (profanity, targeting, threats).

themes.label: Attribution-heavy political naming (proper nouns, handles, institutions)
defining_features: named_proper_nouns_density: dense mentions of political actors/organizations/locations/institutions
quote_or_attribution_embedding or nra_rhetorical_quote_present: attribution plus quotation
hashtag_or_mention_pattern or second_person_direct_address: addressing named individuals via @mention
themes.interpretation: Naming public figures and institutions is common across both groups; on its own it’s not necessarily a moderation trigger, but it increases specificity and can amplify harm when paired with insults or threat-like claims.

themes.label: Mockery / ridicule / dismissive rhetorical tone
defining_features: ridicule_or_mockery: dismissive framing (wishful thinking, clown/joke)
sarcastic_or_outrage_style_rhetoric: rhetorical question used to ridicule
rhetorical_question: recall/argument prompts that function rhetorically
themes.interpretation: Ridicule and mockery are frequent and appear in both keep/remove outcomes, indicating that tone-based dismissal is present broadly; moderation likely depends on whether this combines with stronger harassment/profanity or violent/threat framing.

themes.label: Call to action / political participation and collective mobilization
defining_features: call_to_action: urging others to vote, join, pressure, start movements
policy_prescription_present: prescribes political action steps (forced transparency, voting out, etc.)
themes.interpretation: Collective political exhortations appear in both groups; they become more moderation-relevant when they explicitly target violence/weapon acquisition or demand removal/actions against individuals.

themes.label: Threat-like or violent conditional harm framing
defining_features: policy_prescription_present: directives that imply weapon use or harm toward an addressee (e.g., “would turn their guns on you”, acquire AR out of spite)
call_to_action: spite/weapon acquisition
high-stakes ultimatum style: “When fascism wins, we all die.”
themes.interpretation: Threat/violence-adjacent conditional harm and weaponization intent show up only in removed content here, suggesting this cluster is a strong safety/harms signal.

cross_cutting_themes: Us-vs-them targeting (Theme 2) often co-occurs with profanity/insults (Theme 3) and ridicule (Theme 7).
Policy debate around guns (Theme 1) frequently intersects with victim/persecution and harm narratives (Theme 5) and sometimes with threat-like framing (Theme 9).
Conspiratorial narratives (Theme 4) commonly pair with dense political naming (Theme 6) and aggressive or dismissive tone (Theme 3/7).
Normative moral language (Theme 5) spans many domains (abortion, immigration, climate, justice) and can appear alongside both policy prescriptions and targeting.
